items.prompt: How can a frog take in oxygen directly through its skin?

options.label: Its skin contains tiny gill-like openings connected to the lungs
options.feedback: No gill-like openings run through the skin; oxygen instead crosses the moist skin surface directly into blood vessels lying just beneath it.

options.label: Oxygen dissolves into moisture on the thin skin and passes into blood vessels beneath it
options.feedback: A frog's skin is thin and kept constantly moist, and oxygen from the air or water dissolves into that moisture before diffusing straight through the skin into a dense network of blood vessels just underneath.

options.label: Special pores open and close on command to let air in
options.feedback: No controllable pores exist in frog skin for this purpose; gas simply diffuses continuously through the moist surface wherever it is thin enough.

options.label: The skin stores oxygen as a reserve for the lungs to draw on later
options.feedback: The skin does not act as a storage tank for oxygen; gas exchange there happens continuously and directly into the bloodstream, not by holding a reserve.

items.ok_line: Moist, thin skin lets oxygen diffuse straight into the blood beneath it.
items.ko_line: There are no gills or on-off pores here; think about what a thin, wet surface allows gas to do.
items.exp_title: Breathing through a wet, thin skin
items.exp_text: A frog's skin is thin enough, and kept moist enough by mucus glands, that oxygen dissolved in that surface moisture can diffuse straight through it into a rich network of blood vessels running just beneath the surface. Carbon dioxide leaves the body by the same route in the opposite direction, making the skin a genuine second breathing surface alongside the lungs. This kind of breathing becomes especially important while a frog is submerged and its lungs are of little use, such as resting at the bottom of a pond through the winter.

items.prompt: Why must a frog's skin stay moist at all times for it to breathe properly?

options.label: Gases can only dissolve and diffuse across a wet surface
options.feedback: Oxygen and carbon dioxide need to dissolve into a liquid film before they can pass through the skin at all, so a dry patch of skin simply stops working as a breathing surface.

options.label: Moisture keeps the skin's color bright for camouflage
options.feedback: Camouflage is not connected to why breathing through the skin needs moisture; the requirement is about how gases actually cross the skin, not about how the skin looks.

options.label: A wet skin is lighter, helping the frog swim faster
options.feedback: Swimming speed has nothing to do with why the skin must stay moist; the real requirement concerns how oxygen and carbon dioxide move across it.

options.label: Moisture stops the skin's mucus glands from overproducing
options.feedback: Mucus glands are what keep the skin moist in the first place, not something that moisture itself needs to be controlled to prevent.

items.ok_line: Gases have to dissolve into a wet film before they can cross the skin.
items.ko_line: This is not about color, swimming, or mucus glands; think about what a gas needs before it can pass through a surface.
items.exp_title: Wet is what makes the skin work
items.exp_text: Gases cannot simply pass through dry skin; oxygen from the surrounding air or water first needs to dissolve into a thin film of moisture on the skin's surface before it can diffuse through into the blood vessels beneath. If a frog's skin dries out, that film disappears and the gas exchange happening across it grinds to a halt, on top of the damage drying causes to the delicate skin itself. This is why frogs stay near water or damp shelter and why mucus glands work constantly to keep the surface wet.

items.prompt: How does a frog use its own eyes to help swallow its food?

options.label: It closes its eyes tightly to squeeze saliva down its throat
options.feedback: Saliva production is not what closing the eyes achieves here; the actual effect involves the eyeballs physically moving, not producing any fluid.

options.label: Blinking triggers a reflex that opens the throat wider
options.feedback: Blinking itself is not the trigger for a separate throat-opening reflex; instead, the eyeballs themselves move down and press directly on the food.

options.label: Its eyeballs retract downward into the skull, pushing food toward the throat
options.feedback: When a frog blinks while swallowing, its eyeballs sink down into the roof of the mouth, and this movement physically presses down on the food, helping shove it further back toward the throat.

options.label: Its eyes secrete a digestive fluid that softens the food
options.feedback: No digestive fluid comes from the eyes; what actually helps swallowing is a purely physical push, as the eyeballs themselves move downward into the mouth.

items.ok_line: The eyeballs sink down and physically push the food along.
items.ko_line: No fluid or separate reflex is involved; think about the eyeballs themselves moving.
items.exp_title: Eyes that double as a swallowing tool
items.exp_text: A frog's eye sockets connect to the roof of its mouth, and when it blinks while eating, the muscles around the eyes pull the eyeballs down into these sockets rather than simply closing eyelids over them. As the eyeballs sink, they bulge down into the mouth cavity and press directly against whatever food is sitting there, helping shove it further back toward the throat. A frog swallowing a struggling insect will often blink rapidly and repeatedly, using this motion again and again to work the meal down.

items.prompt: How does a tadpole's body transform into that of an adult frog?

options.label: The tail simply falls off once the legs have finished growing
options.feedback: The tail does not just fall away on its own; its tissue is broken down and absorbed back into the body, driven by the same signal that also drives every other change of metamorphosis.

options.label: A hormone triggers the tail's tissue to be reabsorbed while legs grow and gills give way to lungs
options.feedback: Thyroid hormone rising in the tadpole's body sets off a coordinated set of changes together: gills are replaced by lungs, legs grow out, and the tail's own tissue is broken down and absorbed back into the body rather than being cast off.

options.label: The tadpole grows a completely new body around its old one
options.feedback: There is no new body built around the old one; metamorphosis instead remodels the tadpole's existing tissues and organs directly into their adult forms.

options.label: Warmer water alone is enough to trigger every part of the change
options.feedback: Water temperature can influence how fast development proceeds, but the actual changes themselves are driven by a hormone acting inside the tadpole's body, not by warmth on its own.

items.ok_line: A single hormone drives the whole coordinated transformation.
items.ko_line: Nothing here is built fresh or falls off untouched; look for what could coordinate several changes at once.
items.exp_title: One hormone, several changes at once
items.exp_text: As a tadpole matures, its body begins producing rising levels of thyroid hormone, and this single hormone sets off metamorphosis's several changes together rather than one at a time. Legs grow outward from small buds, gills are gradually replaced by lungs suited to breathing air, and the tail's tissue is broken down cell by cell and absorbed back into the body for reuse rather than simply being shed. By the time the tail has fully disappeared, the same hormone has already reshaped the rest of the body to match its new life on land.

items.prompt: How does a frog's tongue catch a fast-moving insect so quickly and reliably?

options.label: It fires a fine sticky thread rather than the whole tongue
options.feedback: The entire tip of the tongue makes contact with the prey; no separate thread is shot out ahead of it.

options.label: It releases a numbing venom that stuns the insect on contact
options.feedback: No venom is involved in a frog's tongue strike at all; what catches the insect is a sudden shift in the stickiness of its saliva.

options.label: It wraps around the insect using rows of small hooks
options.feedback: There are no hooks along the tongue's surface; the grip instead comes from a saliva that behaves very differently in an instant, not from any hooked texture.

options.label: Its saliva turns watery on impact to flow around the prey, then thickens again as the tongue snaps back
options.feedback: Normally thick, a frog's saliva turns suddenly watery the moment the tongue strikes, letting it flow around the insect's body and into every crevice, then thickens again just as fast as the tongue retracts, trapping the prey firmly against it.

items.ok_line: The saliva itself switches between watery and thick in an instant.
items.ko_line: No thread, venom, or hooks are involved; think about what could change about the saliva itself in a fraction of a second.
items.exp_title: Saliva that switches states in an instant
items.exp_text: A frog's tongue is coated in saliva that behaves like a soft solid most of the time, but the sheer force of impact when the tongue strikes an insect makes that saliva turn suddenly watery, letting it flow around every contour of the insect's body. As the tongue snaps back toward the mouth, the force eases and the saliva thickens again almost immediately, gripping the prey firmly for the rest of the trip inward. This switch between watery and thick happens fast enough that the whole catch is over before the insect has any chance to react.

items.prompt: How does a salamander manage to regrow an entire limb after losing one?

options.label: Cells at the wound site revert to an earlier, unspecialized state and rebuild the limb
options.feedback: At the site of the injury, mature cells lose their specialized identity and gather into a mass of unspecialized cells, which then divide and redevelop into all the bone, muscle and nerve tissue of a complete new limb.

options.label: A spare, half-formed limb is already stored beneath the skin
options.feedback: No pre-formed spare limb waits hidden under the skin; the new limb instead builds up gradually from cells at the wound that only become specialized as it grows.

options.label: Nearby muscle tissue simply stretches to reach the missing part
options.feedback: Stretching existing muscle would not recreate bone, nerves or the other tissues of a limb; a genuinely new limb has to be built from cells that regain the ability to become any of those tissue types.

options.label: The salamander borrows tissue from an unrelated part of its body
options.feedback: No tissue is transplanted in from elsewhere in the body; the new limb grows entirely from cells gathered right at the site of the original injury.

items.ok_line: Cells at the wound revert to an unspecialized state and rebuild from there.
items.ko_line: Nothing is pre-formed, stretched, or borrowed from elsewhere; think about what happens to cells right at the wound.
items.exp_title: Cells that start over at the wound
items.exp_text: When a salamander loses a limb, cells at the site of the wound lose their previous specialized identity, whether they had been muscle, bone or skin, and gather together into a mass of cells capable of becoming any of those types again. This mass then grows and gradually redevelops into the bone, muscle, nerve and skin of a fully functioning new limb, following much the same pattern the original limb once followed while the salamander was still an embryo. Few other animals keep this ability into adulthood the way salamanders do.

items.prompt: How do lungless salamanders manage to breathe without any lungs at all?

options.label: They store oxygen in a reservoir under their tail
options.feedback: No internal oxygen reservoir exists for this purpose; breathing in these salamanders happens continuously through gas exchange at a body surface, not from a stored supply.

options.label: They breathe through gills that stay hidden until needed
options.feedback: Lungless salamanders are not relying on hidden gills as adults; the surfaces doing the work of gas exchange are their skin and the lining of the mouth.

options.label: They exchange gas entirely through their moist skin and the lining of the mouth
options.feedback: With both the skin and the moist lining inside the mouth kept thin enough for gas to cross directly into nearby blood vessels, oxygen enters and carbon dioxide leaves without lungs ever being needed at all.

options.label: They surface periodically to gulp air directly into their bloodstream
options.feedback: No direct route carries gulped air into the bloodstream; without lungs, all of a lungless salamander's gas exchange happens instead through its skin and the lining of its mouth.

items.ok_line: The skin and the lining of the mouth take over the entire job.
items.ko_line: There is no reservoir, hidden gills, or gulped air here; think about what surfaces stay thin and moist enough for gas exchange.
items.exp_title: Two surfaces standing in for lungs
items.exp_text: Lungless salamanders rely entirely on two moist surfaces for gas exchange: their thin skin, richly supplied with blood vessels just beneath it, and the equally thin, moist lining inside the mouth and throat. Oxygen dissolves into the moisture covering these surfaces and diffuses straight into the blood, while carbon dioxide leaves by the same route in reverse, with no lungs involved at any point in the process. Because this depends so completely on staying wet, these salamanders are restricted to consistently damp or aquatic habitats where their skin never has the chance to dry out.

items.prompt: How does a poison dart frog's skin come to be toxic?

options.label: It manufactures the toxin itself from ordinary body proteins
options.feedback: A poison dart frog does not build its toxin from scratch inside its own body; the toxin instead comes from outside, through what the frog eats.

options.label: It absorbs and stores toxins from the ants and mites it eats in the wild
options.feedback: Certain small insects and mites in a poison dart frog's wild diet carry defensive toxins of their own, and the frog absorbs these compounds from its food, storing and concentrating them in glands within its skin.

options.label: Bacteria living permanently on its skin surface produce the poison
options.feedback: No permanent colony of toxin-producing bacteria lives on the skin for this purpose; the toxin's true source is compounds absorbed from the frog's diet.

options.label: The toxin develops automatically as the frog grows older
options.feedback: Age by itself does not produce toxicity; a frog only becomes toxic if its diet actually supplies the toxic compounds in the first place, regardless of how old it is.

items.ok_line: The toxin comes from its diet, not from anything the frog makes itself.
items.ko_line: Nothing is self-made, bacterial, or age-driven here; think about where the toxin could originate outside the frog's own body.
items.exp_title: A borrowed toxin from the diet
items.exp_text: In the wild, poison dart frogs feed heavily on small ants, mites and other tiny invertebrates that themselves carry defensive toxic compounds picked up from what they in turn have eaten. Rather than building any toxin of its own, the frog absorbs these compounds from its prey and concentrates them into glands packed throughout its skin, ready to be secreted if the frog is threatened or handled. A poison dart frog raised in captivity on a diet lacking these particular toxic insects grows up with skin that is essentially harmless.

items.prompt: How does a small frog's mating call carry so far despite the size of the animal making it?

options.label: An inflatable vocal sac acts as a resonating chamber that amplifies the sound
options.feedback: Filled with air as the frog calls, a vocal sac of stretched skin under or beside the throat vibrates along with the sound, acting like a resonating chamber that amplifies the call well beyond what the vocal cords alone could produce.

options.label: The frog vibrates its whole body against the ground to project sound
options.feedback: Ground vibration is not how a frog's call is projected outward; the amplification instead happens through a resonating air-filled sac connected to the throat.

options.label: Water around the frog carries the sound further than air would
options.feedback: Many calling frogs are sitting well above the waterline when calling, and water is not what amplifies the sound in the first place; the true amplifier is the vocal sac itself.

options.label: The frog repeats the same short call thousands of times per second
options.feedback: It is not sheer repetition rate that makes the call carry; the amplification comes from a resonating air-filled sac, not from how quickly the call repeats.

items.ok_line: An air-filled sac resonates and amplifies the call.
items.ko_line: This is not about the ground, water, or repetition speed; think about a part of the frog that inflates with air while it calls.
items.exp_title: An air sac that turns a small call into a loud one
items.exp_text: As a frog calls, it pushes air across its vocal cords and into a sac of stretchable skin under or beside the throat, inflating it like a small balloon. This air-filled sac vibrates in sympathy with the sound produced by the vocal cords, acting as a resonating chamber that reinforces and amplifies the call far beyond what the vocal cords could achieve working alone. The exact shape and size of the sac helps give each species of frog a call with its own particular, recognizable tone.

items.prompt: How can some frogs freeze solid through the winter and still survive?

options.label: Their blood is naturally replaced by a fluid that cannot freeze
options.feedback: No fluid replaces the frog's blood; instead, the frog's own body produces protective compounds that change how freezing happens within it, without ever swapping the blood itself out.

options.label: They dig deep enough underground that the ground there never actually freezes
options.feedback: Depth alone is not what protects these particular frogs; some of them freeze even while quite close to the surface, protected instead by chemical changes inside their own bodies.

options.label: High concentrations of natural sugars in their cells stop ice from forming inside the cells themselves
options.feedback: As the frog begins to freeze, its liver floods its tissues with glucose, concentrating it heavily inside individual cells so that ice forms only in the spaces between cells, leaving the more fragile interior of each cell protected from damaging ice crystals.

options.label: Their hearts keep beating at a reduced rate throughout the freeze
options.feedback: A freezing frog's heart does not keep beating through the freeze; it can stop entirely, and it is the protection of the cells themselves against ice damage that allows the frog to survive that stoppage.

items.ok_line: Concentrated sugar inside the cells keeps ice out of the cells themselves.
items.ko_line: This is not about depth underground or a beating heart; think about what could stop ice from forming in a particular place inside the body.
items.exp_title: Sugar that steers where ice forms
items.exp_text: As the temperature around a freeze-tolerant frog drops, its liver releases a surge of glucose into its bloodstream, and this sugar becomes heavily concentrated inside the frog's individual cells. That high concentration makes it much harder for ice to form inside those cells, so as the frog's body freezes, ice crystals form mainly in the fluid between cells rather than within the more vulnerable cells themselves. With its cells protected this way, a frog can have much of its body turn to ice, its heart included, and still recover fully once it thaws.
